sentences.text: This genus contains only one known species, Pterodromoides minoricensis.
It was a medium-sized bird similar in shape and proportions to modern petrels of the genus Pterodroma.
Like the snow petrel, it possessed a broad nasofrontal hinge, interorbital bridge, and fused prefrontals.
A curved and narrow mark indicating a salt gland is visible on the skull.
The skull features a large orbitonasal foramen and a small postorbital process located above the zygomatic process.
Unlike Puffinus, it had a round humeral shaft without flattening.
The tarsometatarsus lacked the lateromedial compression seen in Puffinus and resembled the proportions of Cookilaria.
Fossils of Pterodromoides were first found at the Punta Nati site on the island of Menorca in the western Mediterranean.
Fossils were excavated from Punta Nati, Menorca, in August 1995 by Josep Quintana and Salvador Moyà-Solà.
The species was named Pterodromoides minoricensis in 2001 based on a skull and postcranial remains.
The holotype for the species is a cranium designated as IPS 11826.
A specimen found in North Carolina suggests the species lived across the North Atlantic.
A partial left humerus found at the Yorktown Formation in North Carolina has been assigned to this species.
It was a seabird that hunted fish and invertebrates, likely feeding on surface prey pushed there by currents or predators.
Evidence from North Carolina and the Mediterranean suggests it was widespread across the North Atlantic and possibly a migratory species.
The genus lived during the Late Miocene epoch.
The species lived between 5.333 and 2.58 million years ago during the Zanclean to Piacenzian ages.
Researchers theorize that its rarity in the Yorktown Formation is due to taphonomic processes related to its surface feeding ecology.
